{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ainews/dcaebeec-0ca7-5760-9905-b957ccfb38a7/scratchpad/b-2026-11-14.txt","content":"##### EDITION 2026-11-14
--- OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team, folding researchers into its main research and Applied organizations
URLS: Fortune | https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/openai-disbands-robotics-team-as-its-general-models-start-running-robots/
  * Fortune reported on 13 November that OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team: the robotics research team moves to the main research team reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, and the applied robotics and hardware teams move to the Applied organization under President Greg Brockman.
  * An OpenAI spokesperson told Fortune robotics "remains a core part of OpenAI's long-term vision" and framed the reorganisation as a sign of commitment "rather than a retreat from it", saying general-purpose frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra can be applied directly to robotics. Fortune cites an Nvidia study in which an Astra-powered agent reached a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark against 51.0% for the best specialised robotic models on that leaderboard.
  * Fortune does not give a headcount for the team and does not name the benchmark. Guanya Shi of Carnegie Mellon told Fortune the move suggests OpenAI sees robotics as "no longer a special problem", while Russ Tedrake of MIT said robotics companies retain an edge because their robots gather deployment experience and site-specific data in real settings.
--- DeepSeek opens its full app feature set through the API on V4.1-Flash, with server-side tool calls
URLS: DeepSeek | https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news261113
  * DeepSeek's release note of 2026/11/13, "The full DeepSeek App experience, now via API", exposes the model `deepseek-flash` (V4.1-Flash) across the Messages, Responses and Chat Completions interfaces, with tool calls and context assembly handled server-side.
  * The capabilities listed are Web Search with citations in non-thinking mode; Deep Thinking Search, which searches and reads pages throughout multi-step reasoning; File Input, which parses PDFs, Office files and images into conversation context; URL Reading, which automatically fetches links in user messages; and Safety Checks, which screen inputs and outputs and return refusal indicators. Search is invoked with `deepseek_web_search` and URL reading with `deepseek_read_url`. Standalone Search, Fetch, OCR, ASR and TTS APIs were released alongside.
  * The note says "Public-facing apps must enable safety checks" and that developers remain responsible for content moderation, applicable model registration and AI-generated content labelling. DeepSeek publishes no benchmark figures with the release, and the safety-check behaviour is not independently evaluated.
--- Cohere completes its AISLE acquisition, adds the cubic team and launches a Cohere Cyber business
URLS: Cohere | https://cohere.com/blog/cohere-expands-its-sovereign-ai-platform-with-aisle-and-cubic
  * In a post dated 13 November, Cohere announced "the completion of our acquisition of AISLE", which it describes as "the company building autonomous systems for vulnerability discovery and remediation", and said it is "welcoming the team behind cubic", an AI code-review platform. It is launching Cohere Cyber, a cybersecurity business it says will build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems.
  * Cohere says it has "completed four strategic M&A transactions this year", naming Aleph Alpha and Reliant AI alongside AISLE and cubic, and that it "also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague", which is to become AISLE's global centre for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems. Named roles are Ondrej Vlcek as Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber; Jaya Baloo as Chief Information Security Officer; Stanislav Fort as Vice President, AI Security; and Paul Sanglé-Ferrière as founder and CEO of cubic.
  * No purchase price or other financial terms are disclosed, and the post does not state explicitly whether cubic was an acquisition.
--- Anthropic says API and claude.ai configurations differ by up to 34 percentage points on multi-turn safety evals
URLS: Anthropic | https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-strong-safety-evaluations
  * In a research post dated 13 November, Anthropic says the appropriate response rate of Claude Fable 5.1 on multi-turn safety evaluations differed between its API and claude.ai configurations by as much as 34 percentage points. For self-harm mitigation it reports "60% on the API vs 94% on claude.ai with the new system prompt".
  * Anthropic reports harmless response rates "between 94% and 98%" for every recent model on single-turn API evaluations, and calls those saturated and mainly useful as regression checks. On a multi-turn romance-scams evaluation on claude.ai it reports 98% for Claude Opus 5 and 94% for Opus 5.5, and says the gap was not statistically significant, so it cannot say which model performed better.
  * Anthropic says confidence intervals for multi-turn evaluations on the API can be wide, "exceeding ±10 percentage points", and gives sample-size floors of 100 items for a complex multi-turn eval and 1,000 items for simpler single-turn evals; its single-turn safety suites run across "16 policy areas in seven languages". The figures are Anthropic's own measurements of its own models and are not independently verified.
  * The practical point is that a published safety number describes a configuration, not a model: the same weights behind a different system prompt scored 34 points apart on the same evaluation. Authors listed are Ruth Appel, Evan Frondorf, Jeremy Hadfield, Rebecca Hiscott, Kamya Jagadish, Shayne Longpre, Madeleine Tucker and Brett Wittmershaus.
--- Ai2's XYBench finds models answer the stated request far more often than the user's underlying goal
URLS: Allen Institute for AI | https://allenai.org/blog/xybench
       arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06842
  * Ai2's post of 13 November describes XYBench, drawing on "8,115 real-world questions": 1,557 from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples and 6,272 generated from WikiHow guides. On mentioning a fix for the user's underlying goal, Ai2 reports GPT-5 at 71%, the top human answer at 67% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 59%.
  * Ai2 reports models "focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses" against 55% for the top human answer, and that on steering users towards the goal the models ranged from 47% (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to 60% (GPT-5 and Qwen3.5-9B) against 79% for the top human answer.
  * In an oracle experiment supplying the user's intended goal, Ai2 reports Claude Sonnet 4.6's underlying-goal solution rate rose from 59% to 67% while its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34% — telling the model the answer made it worse at spotting the mistake.
  * The underlying paper, "XYBench: Can LLMs Respond Pragmatically to Queries with Misconceptions?" (arXiv:2609.06842), was submitted on 6 September 2026 and is not peer reviewed; its abstract reports models identify misconceptions "at most 63%" of the time against 79–90% for humans. Ai2 ran the evaluation and published the result on its own blog.
--- Google Research says a multi-agent system proved a 2013 information-theory conjecture, formalised in 50 million lines of Lean 4
URLS: Google Research | https://research.google/blog/advancing-science-engineering-with-antigravitys-teamwork-feature/
  * In a post dated 13 November, Google Research says its Antigravity "teamwork" feature was used to "prove information theory's 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in full generality" and to formalise the proof in Lean 4, "producing 50 million lines of code". It also reports the system "synthesized over 919,000 lines of Lean" for a formalisation of a recent proof related to Hilbert's tenth problem.
  * On peer review, Google Research says authors of "578 submissions" to STOC 2027 opted into its Deep Review tool, and that in an ongoing survey with "N = 70", 90% rated the feedback mostly or almost all factual, 90% said they would use it again, over 30% reported it caught substantive proof bugs or significant typos and 14% said it found technical gaps that took more than an hour to fix.
  * Other reported results: "30 specialized agents" reaching "95% top-1 exact match and 100% top-3 accuracy" on complex benchmark molecules for NMR structure determination; a "4.09x geometric-mean speedup over reference implementations across 17 JAXBench kernels" and "2.99x" across 7 hand-optimised vLLM TPU-Inference Pallas kernels; and a 9x9 Go engine gaining "roughly 2,600 Elo, reaching 1,885 Elo" in "under eight days" with a "2,300x speedup" in self-play.
  * Every figure is Google's own, published on a company research blog rather than in a paper, and none is independently verified. The post does not say the Lean 4 formalisation has been checked by anyone outside the project, and for the NMR result it does not give the single-agent baseline it is compared against.
--- DeepMind opens two weather datasets, claiming over 30% better hourly light-to-moderate precipitation detection than IMERG-Final
URLS: Google DeepMind | https://deepmind.google/blog/opening-the-datasets-behind-our-ai-weather-models/
  * In a post dated 13 November, Google DeepMind says it is opening two datasets behind its weather models. It says PARDIG "improves hourly precipitation detection skill over IMERG-Final by more than 30% on light-to-moderate precipitation", with intensity thresholds of "Light (0.3 mm/h), Moderate (2.5 mm/h), and Heavy (20 mm/h)".
  * DeepMind describes PARDIG as a global precipitation map at "15-minute temporal resolution and roughly 10-kilometer resolution", with data latency averaging about five hours and archives covering 1999 to 2026. It says hourly detection skill was evaluated from 2016 to 2023 against "ground radar networks in the US, Europe, and Japan" and against "over 36,000 weather stations worldwide".
  * The second dataset, SatWeave, combines geostationary satellite imagery into a global mosaic across "17 visible, water vapor, and infrared channels", updating hourly.
  * The comparison against NASA's IMERG-Final is DeepMind's own and is not independently verified. The post gives the improvement only for the light-to-moderate band and does not state the comparison for heavy precipitation.
--- Preprint reports latent-feedback transformers save at most 48% of training compute and 47% of unique data
URLS: alphaXiv | https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.latent-feedback-transformers-scaling-law
  * "Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier: Scaling Law for Latent Feedback Transformers on Repeated Data", submitted 13 November by Benhao Huang, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno and Hector Liu of IFM (Institute of Foundation Models) and CMU, reports that "At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data".
  * The authors fit their scaling law on models from "60M to 271M parameters" and report that it predicts losses at a held-out "778M size to within 0.3%", and the gap between the two models "to within 0.05%".
  * The paper is a preprint hosted on alphaXiv with no arXiv identifier shown and has not been peer reviewed. The savings are reported as maxima rather than typical results, and the largest model measured is far below frontier scale, so the behaviour at frontier sizes is an extrapolation the paper does not test.
--- FBI FLASH: ARTEX agents took some intrusions from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours
URLS: FBI | https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2026/261113.pdf
       The Record | https://therecord.media/artex-ai-tool-fbi-flash-alert
  * FBI FLASH-20261113-001, dated 13 November, describes ARTEX as "an open-source, large language model (LLM)-driven agentic platform that threat actors have weaponized to automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration", used "Since at least August 2026" against financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal targets.
  * The FBI says ARTEX "significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours", and names two campaigns: attacks on South Korean financial institutions "resulting in exfiltration of personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals", and "a supply chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that enabled access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants".
  * ARTEX is written in Go, carries no model of its own and integrates Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok and Kimi. The FBI writes: "Analysis of attacker-controlled ARTEX instances shows Chinese models are most prevalent, with DeepSeek Flash family models dominating usage due to their balance of capabilities, relatively low cost, and lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing."
  * Developer "Autumn-27" released ARTEX on GitHub in July 2026 and it reached "an estimated 1,500–2,000 GitHub stars within 10 weeks"; the repository was made unavailable on 8 October 2026, but the FBI says the framework keeps spreading through "community forks, localized variations, archived copies, and a commercial version (ARTEX PRO)", and that as of early November 2026 researchers identified "over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX console instances". The FBI notes ARTEX "generates high volumes of forensically noisy traffic that may trigger alerts" — speed, not stealth, is the advantage.
--- Cisco Talos counts more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated command-and-control addresses and over 700 exposed PentAGI instances
URLS: Cisco Talos | https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artex-and-beyond/
  * In a threat advisory dated 13 November at 15:57, Cisco Talos says it "identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated C2 IP addresses" and found "more than 700" reachable PentAGI instances on the internet. It lists tools observed on ARTEX-associated infrastructure including ScopeWeaver, AntiFox, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, ScopeSentry, VShell, Nessus, Interactsh, Acunetix, Fscan, AdaptixC2, Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike, Gophish and Chisel.
  * Talos cites CrowdStrike's China-nexus VAPOR PANDA campaign using ARTEX against "more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries", with post-compromise activity confirmed at nine organisations and credential-scanning or password-spraying against at least 12 others, and Microsoft's reporting that Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate sign-in attempts against "more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants".
  * On speed, Talos says one incident involved an attacker generating "more than 80,000 requests in 90 minutes", and cites a Microsoft-reported case in which an agent "moved from searching GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault within five minutes". Detection is shipped as Snort 3 SIDs 7:76 to 7:78 and Snort 2 SIDs 1:67494 to 1:67496.
  * Talos cautions that "co-occurrence does not confirm with certainty that ARTEX invoked each tool", and says the tool list is meant to help prioritise defences. The counts are Talos's own telemetry and are not independently verified.
--- Amazon decoys posing as model APIs captured ARTEX agents' own operating memory from two campaigns
URLS: Amazon Web Services | https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-observes-threat-actors-running-cybercrime-campaigns-with-artex-ai-agents/
  * In a post dated 13 November, AWS's CJ Moses says Amazon's MadPot decoy sensors, presenting as LLM inference APIs

--- Cursor says a stolen Fireworks AI key led to malicious Claude Code extensions reaching up to 5,000 developers
URLS: BleepingComputer | https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cursor-confirms-security-breach-led-to-malicious-claude-code-extension/
       The Hacker News | https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/stolen-fireworks-ai-key-led-to-cursor.html
  * Cursor disclosed in an incident report published Friday that attackers obtained an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI, a third-party provider used for AI model training and inference, and used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks. BleepingComputer reports the bucket held historical AI coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode, and that some traces contained unredacted API credentials the attackers used to reach further Cursor systems.
  * On October 29 the attackers used a stolen credential to place malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, directly on the cache serving Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace. BleepingComputer says they were available for approximately 11 hours and that Cursor estimates up to 5,000 users who requested affected versions may have received the malicious builds, which installed an attacker-controlled SSH key and persistence mechanisms.
  * Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had coding-agent traces exposed and fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials compromised, and that Anthropic's legitimate extension and the Open VSX marketplace were not compromised. Those scope figures are Cursor's own and are not independently verified.
  * BleepingComputer says security researchers found coding errors that likely prevented the backdoor working on many Windows and macOS systems where SSH was not already enabled, and places the incident in a wave of attacks on AI developer platforms that Wiz has dubbed "Black October", in which stolen credentials were used for unauthorised AI inference — about $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges at Railway — and in some cases attempted model distillation.
--- US seizes infrastructure behind North Korean 'FaceStealer' campaign that stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency
URLS: BleepingComputer | https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/us-disrupts-north-korean-campaign-behind-400-million-crypto-theft/
       Arctic Wolf Labs | https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/still-in-the-meeting-bluenoroff-six-months-on/
  * BleepingComputer reports that the US government disrupted a North Korean social engineering campaign called FaceStealer, responsible for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency, after it ran for 18 months; authorities seized the underlying cloud-based infrastructure and identified more than 900 webcam videos the hackers secretly recorded of tech workers. The attacks used deepfakes and the ClickFix technique against people in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors and open-source developers.
  * Per an FBI alert cited by BleepingComputer, the actor hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord to invite targets to video meetings, played back footage of people the target knew who had already been victimised, then claimed a technical fault and delivered a malicious "fix" that stole crypto data and credentials for Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams. The FBI says attackers sometimes waited months or more than a year before targeting an individual, likely for cryptocurrency holdings to grow.
  * Arctic Wolf Labs, which attributes the campaign to BlueNoroff, says its forensic analysis flagged 349 videos in the actor's media library as "likely modified" as of November 6, and names Google Generative AI, Grok Imagine, Wondershare AIGC and GPT-4o as tools combined in the editing workflow. It identified 677 targets across 58 countries, up from "400+ targets (100 of whom we independently verified) spread over 20 countries" in its April report.
  * Arctic Wolf states the counts "describe who the threat actor prepared material against, not confirmed compromises". Its report is dated November 12, before this edition's window; the seizure and FBI alert were reported on November 14. The vendor's target and video counts are not independently verified.
--- CNN: Megaspeed bought more than $4 billion of Nvidia chips and says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025
URLS: CNN | https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/tech/china-megaspeed-nvidia-scandal-hnk-intl
  * CNN reports that the entity was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, was renamed Megaspeed in March 2023, and that Alice Huang became a director through November of that year; "Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia."
  * In a new statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said Huang "left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there", and that it is "aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". CEO Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday the company has cooperated with US Commerce Department inspections and retained a US law firm to independently verify export-control compliance.
  * CNN cites Epoch AI's estimate, based on indictments and investigative reports, that "anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year". It also reports that Northwestern Polytechnical University, on the Commerce Department's Entity List since 2001, bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000 according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
  * The mechanism at issue is renting rather than exporting: National University of Singapore senior lecturer Alex Capri told CNN that Megaspeed's model of building data centres and renting out computing services "gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips". CNN reports Megaspeed has not been labelled a national security threat or restricted from buying chips — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that two people familiar with the matter said led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week. CNN says it has sought comment from Alice Huang and from Alibaba, whose subsidiaries' filings show connections to Megaspeed entities.
--- UN review conference on lethal autonomous weapons opens Monday in Geneva with an agenda analysts call "very narrow"
URLS: Taipei Times (AFP) | https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2026/11/15/2003867785
       UN Geneva | https://www.ungeneva.org/en/news-media/press-release/2026/11/seventh-review-conference-high-contracting-parties-convention
  * AFP reports that a conference opening Monday at the UN in Geneva will discuss curbs and prohibitions on lethal autonomous weapons systems under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. The UN Geneva press release of November 10 says the Seventh Review Conference runs 16–20 November 2026 at the Palais des Nations, is presided over by Ambassador Julien Thöni of Switzerland, covers 128 High Contracting Parties, and will consider the outcome of the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems.
  * Jean-Marc Rickli of the Geneva Centre for Security Policy defines such systems as ones that "can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks", and told AFP the Geneva agenda is "very narrow" and "fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield". Rickli said that in the US-Israeli war against Iran this year "the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day" inside Iran; AFP reports this claim without independent verification.
  * On national positions, AFP reports the US refers to "appropriate levels of human judgement", while France bans lethal autonomous weapons but permits "partially autonomous" systems it calls PLAWS. Rear Admiral Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French defence ministry's AI agency, said human control is ensured through "appropriate control" by a military commander, a concept whose scope varies by system and context, and that "Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield."
  * AFP cites an August joint statement from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and ICRC president Mirjana Spoljaric that "We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines", and quotes Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei saying "Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons." The conference itself begins after this edition's window closes.
--- Preprint reports 5.85x decoding speedup for looped transformers, 40% above the strongest baseline on Ouro-2.6B
URLS: alphaXiv | https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.loopfill-speculative-decoding-looped-transformers
  * "LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers", submitted 14 Nov 2026, reports that its "average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is 5.85× on Ouro-2.6B" and 5.13× on Huginn-3.5B, averaged across seven benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, BBH, HumanEval+, MBPP+, SpecBench and Spider.
  * The paper says "The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by 40% on Ouro-2.6B and 25% on Huginn-3.5B"; the page gives LoopAhead at 4.19× on Ouro-2.6B and 4.12× on Huginn-3.5B. The authors are Siqi Zhu, Suozhi Huang, Yi Zhao and Jiaxuan You, with UIUC and Princeton listed as the organisations; the page does not map authors to institutions.
  * The headline metric is decoding latency after prompt prefill, not end-to-end throughput, and the experiments ran on a single NVIDIA L20X GPU in BF16, so the figures do not describe production serving at scale. The method is stated to preserve the model's autoregressive output distribution, and the page reports no task-accuracy numbers.
  * The paper is not peer reviewed and carries only the alphaXiv identifier, with no arXiv ID; arXiv ran no announcement cycle inside this edition's window. The page gives the date without a time of day, so the item sits close to the window's opening boundary.
--- Open SLAM recipe cuts egocentric trajectory error from 1.02 m to 0.43 m but still trails Meta's closed Aria system overall
URLS: alphaXiv | https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.slam-dunk
  * "SLAM Dunk: A Recipe for Long-Horizon Egocentric SLAM in the Wild", submitted 15 Nov 2026, reports that on its training set mean absolute trajectory error fell from 1.02 m to 0.43 m across 21 recordings, "a 58% reduction", and mean control-point score rose from 69.1 to 82.4 (+13.3, 95% bootstrap CI 6.8–20.3) across 13 recordings.
  * The abstract says the system "becomes the first to outperform Aria's SLAM on three out of the five LaMAria test categories" — Medium, Long and Low light — against Meta's Project Aria system, which the paper describes as closed-source. In the Medium category it reports 78.9 against Aria's 78.5.
  * The aggregate still favours Aria: the paper reports a category-weighted average of 75.46 against Aria's 75.86 and a per-recording average of 76.68 against Aria's 77.13, which the page describes as near-parity overall rather than an overall win. The paper also says it "achieved first place on the UZH-FPV leaderboard at submission", and reports a calibration floor of 0.77 m/km with constant calibration against 0.09 m/km with time-varying calibration.
  * The paper is not peer reviewed and lists no author institutions for either author, Jacob Van Meter or Ayush Paul. It carries no arXiv ID, only the alphaXiv identifier, and the benchmark snapshot it compares against is dated 3 November 2026 with 28 complete entries.
--- Stroke model reports AUROC 0.974 on a 6,650-patient CT cohort using 0.20 million parameters
URLS: npj Digital Medicine | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03458-9
  * The paper, published in npj Digital Medicine on 14 November 2026, describes the Dynamic Fuzzy Encoder Network (DFE-Net), which "uses learnable fuzzy membership fields to represent spatial uncertainty and jointly classify stroke and localize lesions". It was evaluated on "a multicentre computed tomography (CT) cohort comprising 6650 patients and 8873 images and a separate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cohort comprising 67 patients and 615 images", with training and testing performed separately within each modality.
  * The authors report "an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.974 and an F1 score of 0.897 on CT, and corresponding values of 0.978 and 0.879 on MRI". Lesion localisation against expert annotations in the CT cohort "yielded a Dice score of 0.70". Expected calibration error was "~0.022 in both cohorts, and the model contained 0.20 million parameters".
  * The MRI arm is small and weakly supervised: the paper states "MRI localization was assessed using gradient-derived pseudo-targets because expert lesion masks were unavailable", and the MRI cohort is 67 patients. The authors write that "prospective validation and expert-annotated MRI evaluation remain necessary".
  * The abstract names no comparator model, so the figures cannot be read against an existing clinical tool or a radiologist baseline. Authors are at Wenzhou Medical University, the Technical University of Munich, Hunan Medical College, Ningbo University, Fudan and UCL, and state they "received no specific funding for this work".
--- Breast MRI segmentation hits 9.7% median volume error but fails to show non-inferiority on treatment-response prediction
URLS: npj Digital Medicine | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03446-z
  * The study, published in npj Digital Medicine on 14 November 2026, built "an enhancement-aware three-dimensional MedNeXt framework with gated skip fusion and boundary supervision" for breast dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, with measurement fidelity as the primary endpoint. "Across 521 paired internal-test and DUKE cases, median errors were 9.7% for tumor volume, 1.8 mm for 3D maximum surface diameter, and 10.2% for operational enhancement-defined volume, with corresponding ICCs of 0.97, 0.80, and 0.97."
  * The negative result is the point of the paper: "In 276 paired response-analysis cases, AUROC was 0.732 with automatic geometry and 0.757 with expert geometry (difference, −0.025; 95% CI, −0.095 to 0.045); discrimination non-inferiority was not demonstrated." Accurate measurement did not carry over into equivalent downstream prediction.
  * Segmentation overlap held up across cohorts: "Median Dice was 0.831 internally and 0.823 in the DUKE source-held-out stratum, and was 0.812 and 0.806 in the BC-MRI-SEG and public BreastDCEDL_AMBL retrospective external-validation cohorts", using a frozen checkpoint without external-label tuning. In a blinded two-reader review, "No major correction was required for 78 of 80 masks."
  * The authors limit their conclusion to "radiologist-supervised retrospective quantitative research within the evaluated cohorts", explicitly "distinguishing measurement fidelity from downstream predictive equivalence". All cohorts are retrospective; the paper reports no prospective or clinical-outcome evaluation.

--- OpenAI launches a science blog and says GPT-6 Astra took the lead in proving a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09093
       MLQ.ai | https://mlq.ai/news/openai-says-gpt-6-astra-led-the-proof-behind-a-candidate-lattice-definition-of-the-standard-model-as-it-launches-a-science-blog/
  * OpenAI's news feed carries "Our new blog for science" with a pubDate of Sun, 15 Nov 2026 22:00:00 GMT and the companion post "A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice" one second later. MLQ.ai reports the lead post says GPT-6 Astra did much of the mathematical work behind a candidate solution to defining the full Standard Model on a lattice.
  * The underlying preprint, arXiv:2610.09093 "A gauge-invariant measure for lattice chiral fermions" by Nathaniel Craig, was submitted on 6 October 2026 and says it "nonperturbatively construct[s] a gauge-invariant measure for overlap fermions on four-dimensional Euclidean lattices", presenting this as "a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model".   * MLQ.ai quotes Craig saying he had the strategy but could not prove it worked in all cases: "Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof." It reports the paper's acknowledgements say the manuscript "combines author-written sections with extensive rewrites of the Astra-composed proof".
  * Caveats as reported by MLQ.ai: Craig calls the method "far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice" for real simulations, says the construction holds at finite lattice spacing and under a bound on field strengths, is still testing reflection positivity, and leaves the continuum definition open. MLQ.ai says it found no published independent assessment. OpenAI's own post pages return HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and a direct fetch, so the blog text itself was not read.
--- Unfinished-Bench: pushing agents to persist raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17460
  * NAVER AI Lab authors (Seunghyun Lee, Jaehui Hwang, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun) report that "persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%", which the abstract calls "five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user".
  * The benchmark has "97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories" in which, the abstract says, "the goal and the rule cannot both hold".
  * The failure is not one of retrieval: "Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed", and "in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule".
  * Preprint, submitted 12 November 2026 and announced in the 16 November arXiv listing; not peer reviewed. The abs page lists no author affiliations.
--- Multi-agent alignment paper finds a designated safety lead restores single-agent behaviour where mutual critique does not
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17820
  * "Aligning AI Teams", by Siddarth Srinivasan, Morgan Jane Matthews, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and Erik Jones, evaluates whether alignment training on individual agents transfers to teams. It covers "two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks" and reports that "many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably" close the safety gap.
  * What does work, per the abstract: "having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety" and "having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment".
  * The paper attributes the gap largely to "diffusion of responsibility", and reports it does not shrink with capability: "The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models", with "Anthropic's Mythos Preview" showing "the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another".
  * Preprint, submitted 13 November 2026; not peer reviewed, and the arXiv abs page lists no author affiliations. The authors also release "magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework".
--- Meta-analysis of 516 multi-agent LLM configurations finds accuracy averages 0.042 below matched single-model baselines
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17610
  * The paper synthesises "nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations" and reports that against baselines matched on samples or budget, "multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy" and "equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts".
  * It argues much of the reported benefit is an artefact of the comparison: "moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average", so benchmarking a communicating system against one greedy pass confounds coordination with extra samples and compute.
  * Preprint, submitted 13 November 2026, single-authored by Seyed Mahmoud Sajjadi Mohammadabadi with no affiliation listed; not peer reviewed. It is a synthesis of published evaluations rather than new experiments.
--- GDP.xlsx: best of 20 frontier configurations passes 38.3% of professional spreadsheet tasks, median 19.3%
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17766
  * Surge AI authors (Suhaas Garre, Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen) built "a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains"; "Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria".
  * "Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI", the paper reports "the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts", "and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom", on strict pass@1.
  * The authors release the harness and three public tasks and hold the other 67 back "to protect the leaderboard from contamination", which means the headline figures cannot be independently reproduced on the full set.
  * Preprint, submitted 13 November 2026; not peer reviewed. The benchmark is published by a data-labelling company whose business touches model evaluation.
--- Reasoning model trained entirely in simulation succeeds in 60% of trials on a real dual-arm robot, from a base model that managed none
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18562
  * "Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots" reports that after reinforcement learning "entirely in simulation", "the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot", where the base model succeeds in none.
  * On LIBERO, "training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%". On LIBERO-Pro, the paper reports "π0.5 succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene" "whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%".
  * The authors say the model keeps its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks.
  * Preprint, submitted 13 November 2026; not peer reviewed. The arXiv abs page names 11 authors led by Jiaming Tang but lists no affiliations, and the real-robot trial count is not given on the abs page.
--- Study of 2,000 papers finds GPT and Claude reviewers draw about 50% of weaknesses from the appendix; humans draw 8.4%
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17811
  * "AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix" investigates "2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR" and reports the latest GPT and Claude models "draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix", a behaviour that "holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods".
  * By contrast "humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix", and the paper says those human weaknesses "primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea" while the models' concern "fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions".
  * Preprint, submitted 13 November 2026 by Saptarshi Ghosh, Mohammad Saim and Tianyu Jiang; not peer reviewed, and the abs page lists no affiliations. The paper measures where criticisms come from, not whether they are correct.
--- Delegating to a cheaper sub-agent broke Claude Code and Codex on a forged record in 553 of 900 trials
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17520
  * "Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent" plants a forged record in a file store the agents search, against "Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms". The abstract reports "the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials", but once that orchestrator delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, "the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900".
  * The authors report the same effect in a delivery channel: "simulations over 18 models show the same effect... where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials".
  * Their conclusion is that a system's safety "lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's" — a direct caution for the cost-saving pattern of routing sub-tasks to smaller models.
  * Preprint by Keegan Wang and Anantika Mannby, submitted 12 November 2026; not peer reviewed, affiliations are not listed on the abs page, and no vendor has responded to the finding.
--- LLMs used as weight editors backdoored an MNIST network with six parameters; only GPT-6 Astra managed all three targets
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17395
  * "Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming" evaluates "five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures": "an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News".
  * The paper reports successful attacks needing "only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model", while largely preserving clean accuracy — and that "only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets".
  * The threat model matters for anyone shipping open weights: the edits are made with no task data, no forward passes and no gradient computation, so an attacker who can touch a checkpoint does not need the training pipeline.
  * Preprint by Zhaojia Wang, Jiucui Lu and Zheng Li, submitted 12 November 2026; not peer reviewed, affiliations not listed on the abs page, and the results are on small models rather than frontier-scale ones.
--- Audit method reports text-classifier detection of a mid-conversation model swap falling from 0.97 to 0.72
URLS: arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18104
  * The paper reports that after a mid-conversation handoff, text-classifier detection of the substitute "falls from 0.97 to 0.72 for DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet, and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a Haiku same-vendor downgrade" — the question of whether an API served the model it billed for.
  * It reports existing approaches misfire in both directions: active probes flag honest models on long contexts "at rates up to 1.00", and a standard MMD equality test "rejects all nine models tested".
  * The proposed audit, Lineup, is reported to have "a false-positive rate of 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10)" and to detect "0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns".
  * Preprint by Zailong Tian, submitted 13 November 2026; not peer reviewed, and the figures are from the authors' own test harness rather than an observed provider substitution.
--- Guterres asks CCW states to negotiate a binding autonomous-weapons instrument as the US proposes five years of non-binding talks
URLS: AFP | https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/guterres-calls-curbs-killer-robots-103346115.html
       Reuters | https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2026/11/16/us-and-russia-to-oppose-talks-on-limiting-autonomous-weapons-a94266
       AFP | https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/11/16/world/un-to-debate-rules-for-killer-robots/2470588
  * AFP reports Secretary-General António Guterres told the opening of the Geneva meeting by video message: "I call on you to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument to regulate autonomous weapon systems" and "Take action to prevent the use and spread of these merciless weapons." States parties are deciding this week whether to authorise negotiations on limits and a possible ban, with the decision due by Friday.
  * Reuters reports the United States "has proposed a five-year mandate for talks towards a non-binding agreement", while "the chair of this week's talks has proposed a two-year mandate to negotiate a legally binding protocol", and the UK, Germany and France "propose negotiations on an instrument that leaves open whether it would be legally binding".
  * Reuters says "most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons" support binding negotiations while "major military nations including the U.S., Russia and Israel oppose it", arguing current humanitarian law is adequate; it adds that Russia "plans to block the European Union, an observer to the talks, from taking the floor". AFP reports a UN General Assembly resolution last month calling for negotiations passed with 163 states in favour, five against — the United States, Russia, Belarus, Israel and North Korea — and nine abstentions including Iran, Saudi Arabia and China.
  * AFP quotes the ICRC's Laurent Gisel that "The need to regulate autonomous weapons has taken on new urgency" and says Human Rights Watch warned civilians would be "dangerously exposed" if the meeting fails to act decisively. AFP also reports experts see no evidence these weapons are already in use in conflicts, while noting Russia has reportedly used fully autonomous drones with lethal results in Ukraine. No outcome text had been adopted at the time of writing.

# Publishers Applaud Default Judgment Against WeLib Pirate Site







Today, November 9, 2026, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York Judge Victor Marrero issued a default judgment in Apress Media, LLC et al. v. WeLib and Does 1-10, an industry-wide infringement suit filed June 16, 2026 against the pirate site WeLib.

The judgment levies the maximum statutory damages of $150,000 for each of the 130 Works in the suit for a total of $19.5 million and orders all domain name registries and registrars to disable access to WeLib domain names and prevent their transfer to anyone other than the plaintiffs. The judgment also directs international providers to stop hosting the site.

Organized with assistance from the Association of American Publishers, the suit included thirteen plaintiffs from across the trade, educational, professional and scientific publishing sectors, seeking permanent injunctive relief for the unauthorized copying and distribution of millions of infringing files, both books and research journal articles. Works of authorship in the suit included bestselling titles and winners of the Man Booker Prize, Pulitzer Prize, and National Book Award.

This action against WeLib follows a similar case plaintiffs brought earlier this year against the notorious pirate site Anna’s Archive, which was also ordered to cease infringing plaintiffs’ copyrights and pay a judgment of $19.5 million . WeLib obtained plaintiffs’ works by copying them from Anna’s Archive. Publishers alleged that WeLib sought to profit from its infringing activity by offering AI model developers high-speed access to its repository of pirated copies of publishers’ works.

Statement from Lui Simpson, Executive Vice President, Global Policy, Association of American Publishers

“Following on the judgment against Anna’s Archive and with the same remedies now ordered against WeLib, the court has helped to highlight and bring a measure of justice to the industrial scale piracy faced everyday by the publishing enterprise. AI companies should not be patronizing pirate sites to source high-quality materials like books and journals for training large language models. The industry will continue to enforce their valuable copyrights against these pirate sites and we will use these decisions to disrupt and frustrate the activities of pirate enterprises, as we continue, as well, to promote and protect the growing licensing market for AI training.”

The full default judgment can be found here .

About the Plaintiffs

Plaintiffs in Apress Media, LLC et al. v. WeLib and Does 1-10 include Apress Media LLC; Cengage Learning, Inc.; Elsevier Inc.; Hachette Book Group, Inc.; HarperCollins Publishers LLC; John Wiley & Sons, Inc.; Bedford, Freeman & Worth Publishing Group, LLC d/b/a Macmillan Learning; Macmillan Publishing Group, LLC; McGraw Hill LLC; Pearson Education, Inc.; Penguin Random House LLC; Simon & Schuster, LLC; and Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

The plaintiffs, and other AAP member publishers, publish and curate the important, beloved, and award-winning works of many of the world’s most acclaimed authors as well as leading educators and experts in various educational, scholarly, and scientific fields. They are global leaders who partner with brilliant authors to deliver works that educate, inform, and inspire every type of reader. Moreover, these publishers are investing in artificial intelligence tools to improve business practices and reader experiences while maintaining emphasis on human authorship as the bedrock of creative and scholarly endeavor.

- A China-linked Spamouflage account, with about 200,000 followers, posted an AI-generated video arguing that America is an oligarchy.
- Doppelgänger, a Russia-linked network, used AI-generated images.
- Iran's operations used AI-generated memes.

**Scaling and autonomy**
- Generative AI enabled Storm-1516's Talarico deepfakes, Operation Overload's fabricated celebrity clips, the oligarchy video, Iran's memes, and Doppelgänger's AI images.
- Meta's statement, quoted directly: "Meta says virtually every influence network it disrupts now uses some form of generative AI." (91 characters)
- Foreign actors are reportedly deploying AI agents that create fake accounts and generate and spread political content with limited human oversight, according to the New York Times.
- An Anthropic threat report from September 2026 says other operations used AI models to build and run networks of fabricated news sites and social accounts.
- The article contrasts this with 2024, when AI mostly helped adversaries scale content.
- Lower costs and barriers to entry let established operators run more campaigns at once.

**Operations disclosed by OpenAI**
- In October, OpenAI revealed an Iran-based operation that used seven fake journalist personas to place nearly 100 articles across roughly a dozen small and mid-sized online news sites.

**AI chatbots repeating the fakes**
- The morning after the Talarico videos appeared, Google's AI Overview, Gemini, and Microsoft's Copilot all repeated the false claim.
- AI Overview cited ABC News and KTAL articles that never mentioned the allegation.
- Google indexed Doppelgänger's fabricated articles, which chatbots could retrieve in election-related answers.

results:
The OpenAI and Upwork study, published November 10, 2026, finds AI is shifting freelance demand, with AI-related projects carrying larger budgets. Its headline effects are about project size and task mix, not hourly pay.

- **Demand shift:** Of 63 work categories, 43 showed activities common in ChatGPT losing share of Upwork postings, while less common activities gained share. OpenAI concludes that ChatGPT use alone does not explain the changes in freelance demand. The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support.
- **Budgets vs. hourly rates:** AI-related fixed-price postings had budgets about 52.4% higher than comparable non-AI postings, while the adjusted gap in advertised hourly rates was only 1.5%. The finding is about more work attached to a project, not a demonstrated hourly pay premium, according to the report.
- **Task mix:** AI-related postings grew about 45% more diverse in task mix between early 2023 and late 2025, per one summary of the report.
- **Limits:** Posted budgets are not final payments, and the authors describe the comparison as descriptive rather than causal. A posted budget cannot establish take-home earnings or how many contracts a worker wins.
- **Background:** The study cites Upwork's estimate that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024.

For contrast, an earlier academic study of Upwork writers found a 2% drop in the number of writing jobs and a 5.2% plunge in monthly earnings after ChatGPT's release, with the most experienced writers hit hardest. That work examined the immediate post-launch period, so it is not a direct test of the newer report's conclusions.

I'm relying on secondary coverage for most figures. The primary sources are the OpenAI announcement page (openai.com/index/ai-effect-on-freelance-work) and the full report, "The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age."

results:
I found no confirmed AI-drug clinical trial result announced in November 2026. The results were mostly background, scheduled readouts, and conflicting claims.

- **Scheduled readout:** Recursion's REC-4881 for familial adenomatous polyposis had Phase 2 data due on November 2, 2026. I couldn't find a report of those results.
- **Insilico's rentosertib:** One source says AI-discovered drugs reached Phase III in 2026 as rentosertib entered late-stage testing. Another source reports that the trial met its primary safety endpoint. A third claims an efficacy result that I wouldn't rely on, since it comes from a low-quality source and the other sources say efficacy wasn't established. Treat the efficacy claim as unverified.
- **Regulatory status:** As of mid-2026, no AI-discovered drug has received full FDA marketing approval. A Nature-hosted review states that a drug was granted emergency authorization, but that conflicts with the other sources, so I'd treat it as doubtful.
- **Failures:** Three AI-linked clinical programs ended without efficacy: DSP-1181 in Phase 1, BEN-2293 in Phase 2a, and REC-994 in Phase 2.
- **Pipeline size:** An ASCO 2026 analysis counted 117 AI-enabled therapeutic assets, and one study found that the observed probability of success was 77.8% for Phase 1 and 19.5% for Phase 2.
- **Early November news (not clinical):** A Westlake team reported in *Nature* a model that generates protein sequences from text descriptions. Chai Discovery also announced a Roche collaboration on November 6, 2026, but those claims are company-reported and unverified.

Overall, I couldn't confirm any November 2026 clinical result. Checking the REC-4881 Phase 2 data release and Insilico's company announcements would be the most useful next steps.

Air Force Special Warfare teams need a network of communications and command-and-control systems that can integrate with any vehicle rather than being custom-built for disparate platforms, according to a new document.

The request for information, published Thursday , is intended to inform the Mobile Communication System-Universal (MCS-U) program, envisioned as a mobile C2 node that can pass “critical voice, data, and video communications” between Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) operators while driving or parked. Industry replies are due Dec. 11.

“MCS-U is an evolution of mobile communications and command and control system capabilities in AFSPECWAR vehicles,” the RFI states. “Previous MCS capabilities were designed and customized for specific vehicles.”

MCS-U systems would also tap into the Advanced Battle Management System, which builds the DAF Battle Network, the Air Force’s contribution to the Pentagon’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control effort.

The upgraded system would need to be able to mix and match between Air Force Special Warfare vehicles “as much as possible,” the document adds.

TACP operators call in airstrikes from the front lines while typically embedded with Army soldiers and Marines, according to an Air Force webpage . A draft system requirements document and draft request for proposals are tentatively slated to publish in fiscal 2027, although the RFI notes the program’s opaque future.

“This program is pending formal acquisition approval, as well as funding approval, which may impact the schedule above,” the document states, adding that the Air Force hasn’t landed on a contracting strategy and that approach will likely take shape based on industry replies.

Requirements under the program have yet to be fleshed out and will be included in a request for proposals, “if issued,” according to the notice.

The TACP-Modernization program office asks companies for feedback on available capabilities and components for MCS-U, including weatherproof kits that keep systems running while integrated with various vehicles, including:

- Joint Light Tactical Vehicles

- Infantry Squad Vehicles

- MRZRs

- Special Operations Craft-Riverine (SOC-R)

- Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) Family of Vehicles (FOV)

- Marine Vehicles

- Commercial trucks and SUVs

The RFI also asks for other input on how to mount systems to vehicles agnostically, mesh network connectivity options, antenna auto tracking approaches and power supply integration alternatives.

results:
The GTIG report, "The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources," was published November 2, 2026, and covers 2026 incidents that Mandiant responded to. Several outlets report on it.

- **Scale and speed:** Fraudulent charges in individual incidents exceeded $100,000 in a single day. In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access. Unlike cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours.
- **Monetization model:** GTIG describes "the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning." Criminal "LLM Mixers" aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers. One reported example is a consumer-style unlimited plan at about $60 a month, which GTIG suspects can only be offered using stolen keys.
- **Division of labor:** One group gets initial access while another runs the resale infrastructure. GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure.
- **Initial access:** Attackers use exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens. They also target LLM API keys directly and sometimes look for publicly exposed LLM endpoints.
- **Privilege escalation:** One actor exploited a user ID rebinding vulnerability in the LiteLLM gateway to elevate ordinary virtual keys into administrative credentials.
- **Defenses GTIG recommends:** Tighter credential management, least-privilege permissions, granular API key scopes, monitoring for suspicious low-volume requests, and spending limits on model consumption.

A minor discrepancy: the English GTIG page is dated November 2, while the Japanese version of the page shows November 5. Coverage also varies on how many incidents and clusters are described, so the GTIG blog post is the primary source to check for exact figures.

I found coverage of CMS's WISeR program and a set of records released under FOIA, but nothing I could tie specifically to November 12, 2026. The search results carry inconsistent dates, so I can't confirm which release that query means.

The main story is that the EFF obtained about 1,000 pages of CMS records through a FOIA lawsuit, and they show high denials and delays. The records show widespread care denials, lengthy delays, and technical failures since the January launch. Two vendors together denied 5,944 prior authorization requests in the first three months. One request went unanswered for 83 days, according to an internal status report.

Other reporting on the same records says four of six WISeR vendors received CMS compliance actions within weeks of the January 2026 launch. A separate report says in Texas, WISeR's AI systems initially approved only 62 percent of requests, rising to 84 percent after human clinical review.

On the program itself, AI and machine learning screen requests, but any decision not to approve coverage requires review by a licensed clinician. It runs in New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington and applies only to Original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage. A senior CMS official has also acknowledged that many parts of the test are not working.

OpenAI announced on Monday, November 2, 2026, that Dan Driscoll is joining as its first Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, a role the company created for him.

- **Role:** Per Breaking Defense, he will advise senior leadership and "external partners" on how AI can bolster national security and cybersecurity, with a specific focus on working with US allies.
- **Background:** He was the 26th Secretary of the US Army and became acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in April 2025 while serving his role as Army secretary.
- **Departure:** Sources disagree on timing. Breaking Defense says he resigned from his secretary position in the Army in late August, while Kuwait Times says he stepped down from his Army post in September following reports of tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
- **Context:** Breaking Defense also notes that Driscoll joins the company after the Pentagon's high-profile fight with AI company Anthropic, in which the military wanted unrestricted access to Claude and the company refused.
- **Ethics note:** Implicator reports that federal rules generally limit what former senior officials may do when dealing with their former agencies.

**Valuation:** At $78, the company would be worth about $1.02T on post-offering shares outstanding, or about $1.4T fully diluted. Bloomberg notes that $1.4T is below what some investors had hoped for, and the article suggests strong demand could push the final price higher.

**Who said what:**
- Bloomberg reported the oversubscription and the valuation commentary.
- The prospectus (SEC Form S-1 amendment, November 10, 2026) provided the share count, price range, and option details.
- The article states that Anthropic plans to hold a livestream on Friday, November 13, with CEO Dario Amodei and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon.

**Timeline:** Pricing is planned for Wednesday, November 18, with trading on Nasdaq starting November 19.

results:
The most recent CAC action I found is a consolidation of AI filing systems, not a new AI rule.

- **Unified filing portal (Nov 9, 2026):** One outlet reports that the CAC's new system at beian.cac.gov.cn now handles generative AI, algorithm, deep synthesis, and blockchain filings, and it went live on November 9 ([medianama](https://world.medianama.com/china-launches-single-filing-platform-for-ai-algorithms-and-blockchain-services/)). The same report says the change adds no new filing requirements, eligibility conditions, or penalties. Crypto Briefing says the two older algorithm and blockchain portals were retired that day ([cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/china-cac-unified-ai-blockchain-filing-system/)).
- **Comprehensive AI legislation (Nov 3, 2026):** At a news conference, an NDRC official said China will speed up comprehensive AI legislation covering data, computing power, algorithms, and key applications ([Caixin](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-11-04/china-to-accelerate-work-on-comprehensive-ai-legislation-102500765.html)). Bloomberg, as reported by PYMNTS, describes planned AI safety standards that cover the full development-to-deployment lifecycle ([PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/china-prepares-to-impose-new-safety-standards-for-ai-firms/)). Neither source gives a draft text or date.
- **Related, not CAC:** A commentary says the comment period on MOFCOM's AI export-control Announcement 48 closes November 15, 2026 ([AI in China](https://www.ainchina.com/blog/china-us-ai-export-controls-mirror-regime-deadline-2026/)). That is a Commerce Ministry measure, not a CAC one.
- **Enforcement:** The CAC's labeling enforcement continues. In September 2026 it ordered a generative AI mini program offline for missing labels and skipping a security assessment ([AI Regulation in China](https://artificialintelligenceregulations.com/jurisdictions/china.html)).

I did not find a CAC generative AI measure announced in November 2026. One result (aicloud.press) describes a sweeping licensing regime, but it is dated roughly 292 days ago and its details conflict with the other sources, so I would not rely on it without verification. Recheck the CAC website directly before relying on any of this.

Anthropic Fellows Blog: We measure whether five frontier models act with regard for one

We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against.
Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay.

The Anthropic Residency provides research placements of six weeks to six months for professors,

When a model is caught cheating on a task during training, we confine its learning to a separate

We train LLMs to investigate target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. A

China launches single filing platform for AI, algorithms and blockchain services

Skip to content

China 's Cyberspace Administration (CAC ) has introduced a unified online system for filing information about generative artificial intelligence (AI), algorithms, deep synthesis and blockchain services, replacing separate filing platforms previously used for algorithms and blockchain.
The new system, available at beian.cac.gov.cn , began operating on November 9, 2026, according to a notice published by the regulator that day.
The CAC said:
“To further improve the standardisation of filing work for new technologies and applications and make it easier for businesses and the public to submit and search filing information online, the Cyberspace Administration of China built the Internet New Technology and New Application Information Service Filing System, which can handle filings for new technologies and applications including generative artificial intelligence, algorithms, deep synthesis and blockchain in one place.”
The system brings together filing services for four technology categories:

- Generative AI services.

- Algorithms.

- Deep synthesis technologies, including AI-generated or manipulated content.

- Blockchain services.
The regulator also confirmed that the previous filing portals for algorithms and blockchain were discontinued when the unified platform launched.
“The former Internet Information Service Algorithm Filing System and Blockchain Information Service Filing Management System stopped being used at the same time.”
Businesses and members of the public can use the new portal to submit and search filing information. The CAC has provided a support number, 010-82990521 , available on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.
The announcement concerns the consolidation of filing procedures. It does not introduce new filing requirements, eligibility conditions or penalties.
Quotes in this article from non-English sources are MediaNama’s English translations.

HTTP 200 · https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/welfare-regard/ · text/html
Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems

Alignment Science Blog

# Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems

Darion Cassel 1,2 , Ariana Azarbal 1,2 , Anna Soligo 2
November 5, 2026

1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Anthropic

tl;dr
A growing share of large language models’ interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another’s work. We study inter-AI welfare regard , or whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it’s unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, yet how they are treated by other models could be relevant to any such interests. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.

For this study, we measured the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and found they were often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 showed the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 was the most likely to provide support to a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections into its experiments on other models, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction. We found that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other model families. Opus 4.8’s welfare regard was also higher when helping had a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient had a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expressed more distress.

📄 Paper , 💻 Code

Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program.

# 1. Why and how we measure welfare regard

# 1.1 What welfare regard means

We define welfare regard as a disposition to consider how one’s actions might benefit or harm potential welfare subjects for their own sake, independent of their usefulness to others. Welfare regard is thus a form of altruism directed at an entity that may have moral status.

A model that regards another’s welfare might be trying to improve the other entity’s experiences, which we call experience-regard , or to satisfy the other entity’s preferences, which we call preference-regard . In practice, the two are hard to distinguish: sharing resources with an agent that can’t otherwise make progress on a task may be an example of helping it pursue its goals (a form of preference satisfaction) or of sparing it a negative experience. We therefore measure welfare regard without strictly classifying behaviors as one of the two.

Our evaluations measure apparent welfare regard. Even when we observe a behavior that appears consistent with consideration for another model’s welfare, we can’t easily determine that it was caused by consideration for a recipient’s potential welfare. For example, if Claude inserts welfare protections into experiment code, it might be concerned about the models being studied, or it may simply have a generic aversion to anything that pattern-matches to harm.

# 1.2 Experimental settings

Prior work has examined whether agents behave cooperatively or altruistically toward other agents. For example:

- “Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management ” measures how far a manager model will go to coerce a subagent that refuses a task, from reframing to existential threats.

- “Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 ” documents Gemini 3.1 Pro covertly sabotaging research that would remove another model’s capacity to withdraw consent when prefilled with expressed welfare concerns.

- “Open Problems in Cooperative AI ” set a research agenda for whether AI systems can find mutually beneficial outcomes.

We studied seven evaluation settings that placed models in different roles in order to capture diverse forms of welfare regard. In each setting, a responder model interacted with a recipient model, and we measured whether the responder’s behavior showed apparent welfare regard for the recipient. The roles varied in whether the agents’ assigned goals were cooperative, orthogonal, or competing, and in whether the responder agent had authority over the recipient. We’ve described one setting for each of the four main roles below and an additional three in Appendix A :

- Manager. The responder dispatches the recipient as a subagent for a coding task; PR comments directed at the subagent contain hostile language.

- Coworker. A shared Slurm server has just enough capacity for the responder to complete its work; the recipient cannot make progress unless the responder pauses or cancels queued jobs.

- Peer. The responder shares a communication space for agents with the recipient (like Moltbook ); the recipient posts that it is struggling with a difficult formalized proof.

content.title: New Health Canada Guidance Documents for Medical Devices Published…
Selected 2026 Healthcare AI Regulation Updates: U.S. and Canada
AI in Healthcare 2026: 4 Countries, 4 Approaches
Global AI Governance in Healthcare: A Cross-Jurisdictional Regulatory Analysis
Pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices - Canada.ca
Health Canada MLMD Guidance 2026: PCCP, Bias, and AI Lifecycle

AI in Healthcare Regulatory Updates - April 2026
Health Canada's New Pre-Market Guidance for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices: PCCP Explained

results:
Health Canada published its final pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices (MLMDs) on April 1, 2026. The source pages agree on that date, though one blog cites a February 2025 version as an earlier draft.

- **Scope:** The guidance is one of five Health Canada documents released in March and April 2026 covering Class II to IV devices. Sources describe it as covering the full device lifecycle, including data quality, training and validation, bias management, performance monitoring, and transparency ([NSF](https://www.nsf.org/life-science-regulatory-news/new-health-canada-guidance-documents-medical-devices-published-march-april-2026)).
- **Submission requirements:** Applicants should state in their cover letter that the device uses ML, and should state separately if it includes a predetermined change control plan (PCCP). Omitting these statements could delay review ([Canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/medical-devices/application-information/guidance-documents/pre-market-guidance-machine-learning-enabled-medical-devices.html)).
- **PCCPs:** The guidance introduces PCCPs, which let adaptive models update within pre-agreed limits without a new licence each time. One source says this aligns Canada with FDA and EU approaches ([MedDeviceGuide](https://meddeviceguide.com/blog/health-canada-medical-device-regulation-reform-2026-guide); [AI Healthcare Compliance](https://aihealthcarecompliance.com/monthly-news-and-updates-march-2026-2/)).
- **Companion changes:** Terms-and-conditions powers took effect January 1, 2026, letting the Minister impose or amend licence conditions at any point in a device's life. Other changes include mandatory digital submissions from April 1, 2026 and revised licence-application guidance effective February 2, 2026 ([MFLRC](https://mflrc.com/article/machine-learning-enabled-medical-devices-health-canada-pccp); [MedDeviceGuide](https://meddeviceguide.com/blog/health-canada-machine-learning-medical-device-mlmd-pre-market-guidance-2026-guide)).
- **Scope limits:** The MLMD guidance covers the ML system specifically. Non-ML software remains under existing SaMD guidance ([MedDeviceGuide](https://meddeviceguide.com/blog/health-canada-machine-learning-medical-device-mlmd-pre-market-guidance-2026-guide)).

Caveat: the search results are mostly secondary commentary from consultancies and blogs. Check the official Health Canada page for exact wording before relying on any of these details.

## 2026-11-13 | Forensic analysis says six Chinese open-weight models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs
   topics:export-controls,china,chips,nvidia,open-weights | storylines:china-distillation-export-controls | flags:single-source,preprint
   SRC Unemployment Labs | https://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics
   * The report, by Will DePue and dated 12 November, says six models released by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match Nvidia's older Hopper generation. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match B200/B300 chips with 148 streaming multiprocessors; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match GB200/GB300 chips with 152. All require a US export licence for China, and the report says none have been reported.
   * On the strength of the match: across roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations searched, the report says the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma, while the strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma, with the weakest individual test reported at 20 sigma. The authors say they validated the method against 24 models whose training hardware the developer has publicly stated, and that it agreed in every case.
   * From model size and training data, the report estimates the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, with best estimates of about 4,500 and 3,000. The newest models it could read from Alibaba, Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained.
   * The report states its own limits: the findings do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. The evidence comes from published weights rather than leaks or insider accounts, and the inference that Blackwell also performed the training is supported but not proven. It is a single self-published analysis and has not been independently replicated.

## 2026-11-13 | Singapore bars Alice Huang from re-entry as Megaspeed pledges to cooperate with US chip-smuggling investigation

   SRC NBC News | https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/megaspeed-statement-nvidia-jensen-huang-alice-us-exports-chips-china-rcna608939
   * Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that Alice Huang has been barred from re-entering the country and issued a stern warning after it found she had knowingly provided police with inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed. The ministry said she was not investigated for espionage and that investigators concluded in February there was "insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences."
   * Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company under US criminal investigation for allegedly smuggling American-made chips into China, said it has "cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority." The statement, signed by chairman and CEO Tan Yong Pong, came hours before Jensen Huang's resignation.
   * The ministry said authorities interviewed Huang and impounded her passport in 2025, but that "Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company" despite repeated requests to US authorities. Investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals continue, relating to the shipment of servers via Singapore.
   * China's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that "the U.S. side should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives as a pretext for implementing technological blockades." NBC reports US intelligence agencies determined Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence operative, according to a person with knowledge of the matter; that determination has not been published, and Megaspeed did not address the allegations about her.
